title: Museum Shop Trends: Five Ideas to Test
content:
Museum shops can introduce visitors to local makers, extend an exhibition’s story and generate income for the institution. They also have to make practical retail decisions about stock, pricing, access and the time available to their teams.

A useful starting point is to choose one change that fits your museum and test it. Better product information, a small local-maker range or clearer online collection options may be more useful than an expensive new retail feature.

Here are five areas to consider when developing a museum shop, with examples and questions to help you decide what is worth trying.

Responsible sourcing starts with details: materials, packaging, manufacturing and the evidence behind the supplier’s claims. A museum shop can help customers understand those details, but it should avoid calling a product sustainable without explaining why.

The British Museum shop provides a concrete example. Its Great Wave foldable tote bag is described as being woven from 100% recycled polyester and is inspired by Hokusai’s print. The product page gives a material specification and a collection connection. That is more useful to a buyer than a broad environmental label.

title: Museums Don’t Need More Visitors. They Need More Contributors.
content:
Above: Anna Stolyarova with the mural Tolerance

On a wall in Amsterdam’s Nieuw-West district, a mural called Tolerance is fading away. Nobody is rushing to restore it. And yet it is still part of a museum collection.

That collection belongs to Street Art Museum Amsterdam (SAMA), a museum without a building. Its hallways are the neighbourhood’s streets. Its artworks are the walls. Its visitors are the people who live there, who are also its contributors and, as founder Anna Stolyarova likes to point out, its sharpest critics.

A museum whose collection is quite literally vanishing has had to face questions most institutions can put off. Who creates cultural value? Who decides what is worth passing on? And what is a museum for when the knowledge it needs already exists outside its walls? SAMA’s approach to citizen science in museums offers a challenge to the whole sector: let residents help shape what the museum knows, preserves and values.
